title: Can you speak Chinese?
goal: Tell apart three Mandarin words that all translate as "can" — 會, 能, 可以 — a point almost every English speaker misses.
bekal: choose correctly between 會, 能, and 可以
ask for permission and turn down requests politely
talk about your skills and how good you are

dialogs.title: 對話 — 借腳踏車
dialogs.intro: Budi wants to borrow A-Ming's bike to go to the morning market, but there's a small problem.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [阿明|Ā Míng]，[我|wǒ][可以|kěyǐ][借|jiè][你的|nǐ de][腳踏車|jiǎotàchē][嗎|ma]？
lines.id: A-Ming, can I borrow your bike?
lines.literal: A-Ming, I — may — borrow — you — 's — foot-pedal-vehicle — (question)?

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.id: Of course. Can you ride a bike?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Sure I can! In Indonesia I ride every day.
lines.literal: know-how — (wow)! at — Indonesia — I — every-day — ride.

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.id: Then no problem. But it's raining today, you know.
lines.literal: then — not — have — problem. but — today — fall-rain — (you know).

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: You can still ride in the rain, right?

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.id: You can, sure, but it's dangerous.
lines.literal: able — is — able, but — will — very — dangerous.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Then I'll just take the MRT.

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.id: Smart! Do you have an EasyCard?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Yes, but I don't know how to top it up.
lines.literal: have, but — I — not — know-how — add-value.

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.text: [很|Hěn][簡單|jiǎndān]！[在|Zài][便利商店|biànlì shāngdiàn][就|jiù][可以|kěyǐ]。
lines.id: It's really easy! You can do it at any convenience store.
lines.literal: very — simple! at — convenience-store — just — can.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [太好了|Tài hǎo le]！[你|Nǐ][真的|zhēn de][很|hěn][會|huì][幫|bāng][人|rén]。
lines.id: Great! You're really good at helping people.
lines.literal: too — good — (now)! you — truly — (one) — very — good-at — help — people.

notes: ⚠️ **不會啦 here means "oh, not at all" — not "can't".** It's the Taiwanese way to deflect a compliment, alongside 哪裡哪裡. You'll hear it every time you praise someone.
**能是能，可是… is the very useful "sure…, but…" pattern**: *好是好，可是太貴。* ("It's nice, sure, but it's too expensive.") Repeat the word with 是 in the middle, then push back with 可是.
⚠️ **The 悠遊卡 (EasyCard) is the one thing you most need in Taiwan.** It works on the 捷運, buses, trains, YouBike public bikes, and for shopping at 便利商店. Buy it and top it up at any convenience store.
**腳踏車 ("foot-pedal vehicle") is the Taiwanese word for bicycle.** Mainland textbooks teach 自行车; using it in Taipei is understood but marks you at once as a mainland-textbook learner.
**很會 + verb means "to be good at something"**: 他很會唱歌 (he's a good singer), 你很會買東西 (you're a great shopper). ⚠️ Different from plain 會, which just means "can".

grammars.title: ⚠️ 會, 能, 可以: three "cans" you can't swap
body: English uses one word, "can", for three very different things: a learned skill, an ability available right now, and permission. Mandarin keeps the three apart, and picking the wrong one is heard at once.

head: Word
Core meaning
Example
Translation
rows: You can top up at a convenience store.

after: **Quick test:** if "can" could become **"know how to"** → 會. If it could become **"be able to"** or **"manage to"** → 能. If it could become **"may"** or **"be allowed to"** → 可以.
⚠️ **我不會去 and 我不能去 are very different.** The first means "I won't go" (a decision); the second means "I can't go" (something's in the way). Mixing them up could offend a friend.
**Answering: repeat the helping verb.** *你會說中文嗎？* → **會** or **不會**. *我可以借嗎？* → **可以** or **不行**.

grammars.title: Asking for permission and saying no
body: Ask for permission with 可以…嗎？ or the softer 可不可以…？ Saying no has several levels, and refusing too directly is considered rude in Taiwan.

head: 中文
Pīnyīn
Meaning
Tone
rows: I'm afraid that might not work

after: ⚠️ **不行 sounds firm and can sting** when said to a friend. Taiwanese people more often say 不太方便 or 可能不行耶 — refusing while leaving room. It's much like the English "that might be a bit tricky".

**Prohibition signs use 禁止 (*jìnzhǐ*, forbidden) or 請勿 (*qǐng wù*, please don't)**: 禁止吸菸 (no smoking), 請勿飲食 (no eating or drinking — ⚠️ enforced throughout the Taipei 捷運, even for water, and the fines are real).

blocks.title: How good are you?
items: **我會一點。** — I can speak a little. (safest and most common)
**我會一點點。** — I can speak a tiny bit.
**我說得不好。** — I don't speak it well.
**我聽得懂，但是不會說。** — I understand, but I can't speak it yet.
⚠️ **Don't answer 我會中文 confidently** if you're still at A1 — Taiwanese people will switch to full speed at once. *我會一點* keeps the conversation slow.

head: 中文
Pīnyīn
English
rows: Could you help me for a moment?
Excuse me, can I get through?
I don't know how to use it

blocks.text: ⚠️ **一下 after a verb softens a request** into "just for a moment": 幫我一下 (help me a sec), 看一下 (take a quick look), 等一下 (wait a moment). Without 一下, your request sounds like an order. Add it to every request until it becomes a habit.
Besides "can, having learned it", 會 also expresses **future likelihood**. What follows tells the two meanings apart: a skill verb → "can"; an event → "will".
⚠️ **Mandarin has no future tense.** The future is marked by time words (明天, 下星期) or helping verbs like 會 and 要. The verb itself never changes at all — no "-s", no "-ed", nothing.

items: Could you help me for a moment?

Answer the questions by repeating the helping verb.
